summary: This standards-track document defines how to run NETCONF inside a Secure Shell session as an SSH subsystem. SSH supplies authentication and protection for the configuration messages. It replaces RFC 4742.

plainLanguage.summary: NETCONF messages need a safe pipe. This says to use an SSH connection, which already locks and checks identity, as that pipe.

questions: what port does netconf over ssh use
what is the netconf ssh subsystem
subtitle: Run NETCONF as an SSH subsystem on TCP port 830, with a framing scheme that fixes the old ]]>]]> separator.

tldr.problem: NETCONF is defined to be independent of its transport, so it needs a concrete mapping onto something that provides authentication and encryption. The earlier mapping used a message separator that can legally appear inside XML.
tldr.mechanism: The NETCONF client opens an SSH session channel and invokes a subsystem named netconf, normally on TCP port 830. After the hello exchange, peers that both advertise base:1.1 switch to chunked framing, where each chunk carries an explicit length.
tldr.outcome: SSH supplies server and client authentication and strong encryption for configuration traffic. This RFC obsoletes RFC 4742.

today: RFC 6242 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2011. It obsoletes RFC 4742, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The NETCONF protocol (RFC 6241) is an XML-based protocol for managing the configuration of networking equipment. It is session-layer and transport independent, so each transport needs a mapping. This RFC defines the mapping for Secure Shell: NETCONF runs inside an SSH session, using the SSH connection protocol (RFC 4254) over the SSH transport protocol (RFC 4253).

The mapping lets NETCONF be run from a secure shell session by a user or application. It is not limited to the example messages shown; it can carry any NETCONF message.
sections.plainLanguage: NETCONF is a language for telling network gear how to set itself up. This document says how to carry those messages safely inside an SSH connection.

sections.title: Starting NETCONF over SSH
sections.content:
The SSH client first sets up an SSH transport connection, and the two sides exchange keys for message integrity and encryption. The client then uses the ssh-userauth service to authenticate the user (RFC 4252), and next the ssh-connection service. It opens a channel of type session, and the NETCONF client invokes NETCONF as an SSH subsystem called netconf.

Using a subsystem means a script does not have to recognize shell prompts or skip extraneous output such as a start-up system message. Subsystems are a feature of SSH version 2 and are not in SSHv1. The SSH username is passed to the NETCONF layer unmodified. If it cannot be represented in XML, the SSH session MUST be dropped.

Servers MUST default to offering the netconf subsystem only on the IANA-assigned TCP port 830, so firewalls can easily identify and filter the traffic. Servers SHOULD be configurable to allow other ports. The RFC's example command line is ssh -s server.example.org -p 830 netconf.
sections.plainLanguage: First you log in to a locked building (SSH). Then you ask for one particular room, named netconf, and speak only the NETCONF language in there. The door for that room is normally number 830.

sections.title: Capabilities Exchange
sections.content:
As soon as the session is established, each side sends an XML <hello> element listing its capabilities. The client's hello is the first XML document the client sends. Both sides send at once, perhaps simultaneously, so neither waits for the other.

After the hello messages, the client sends complete XML documents containing <rpc> elements and the server answers with documents containing <rpc-reply> elements. The capability urn:ietf:params:netconf:base:1.1 matters here because it decides which framing is used next.
sections.plainLanguage: When two people meet they say hello and say what they can do. Here both sides do it at the same time, then take turns asking and answering.

sections.title: Chunked Framing
sections.content:
The first RFC used the character sequence ]]>]]> as a message separator on the assumption that it could never occur in well-formed XML. That was wrong: it can legally appear in XML attributes, comments and processing instructions. The fix keeps compatibility with existing implementations. The <hello> message MUST still be followed by ]]>]]>. If both peers advertise :base:1.1, chunked framing is used for the rest of the session. Otherwise the old end-of-message method is used.

In chunked framing a message is one or more chunks followed by an end-of-chunks marker. Each chunk is a line feed, a hash sign, a decimal chunk size, another line feed, then that many octets of data. The marker is line feed, two hash signs, line feed. Leading zeros are prohibited in the size, and the maximum chunk size is 4294967295.

If the chunk size is invalid or decoding fails, the peer MUST end the NETCONF session by closing the SSH channel. Implementations MUST ensure they are not vulnerable to a buffer overrun.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a special stop sign that might show up inside a letter by accident, each piece of the message starts with its length, like 'the next 18 letters are the message'. Then the receiver just counts.

sections.title: End-of-Message Framing
sections.content:
The end-of-message mechanism exists for backward compatibility with implementations of earlier versions. It is used only when the other peer does not advertise a base version that supports chunked encoding, that is, when it supports only :base:1.0.

In this mode, both client and server MUST send the sequence ]]>]]> after each message (XML document). Anything between the separators is passed up to the messages layer.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the old way: put a special mark after every message. It stays so that older devices can still talk to newer ones.

sections.title: Closing the Session
sections.content: NETCONF is exited with the <close-session> operation. The server processes messages in the order received. When it processes <close-session>, it SHALL respond and close the SSH session channel, and it MUST NOT process any messages received after that operation.
sections.plainLanguage: When you say goodbye, the server answers once and hangs up. It ignores anything you say after goodbye.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
NETCONF reads and changes configuration and state, so access should be limited to authorized users and systems. The SSH client MUST verify and authenticate the SSH server's identity, according to local policy, before sending password-based authentication data or any configuration or state data. The server MUST likewise verify the client's identity before any configuration or state data is sent to or received from it. Neither side should connect to an unknown, unexpected or incorrect peer.

Configuration data can include sensitive items such as usernames or security keys, so NETCONF needs strong encryption, which this mapping supports. The fixed port makes traffic easier for firewalls to filter, but also easier for attackers to spot. Using another port without matching firewall changes could unintentionally expose the subsystem to nodes outside the firewall.

The end-of-message sequence can cause operational problems and open the door to attacks if sent deliberately inside RPC messages, though the RFC says the threat is believed not to be very high. Chunked framing is used after the hello to avoid injection attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must check who they are talking to before sharing anything, because the messages can hold secrets. The new counting method also stops sneaky tricks with the old stop sign.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 4742
sections.content:
This RFC obsoletes RFC 4742. The main changes are the new chunked framing mechanism to fix the security problems of end-of-message framing, extended Security Considerations, added examples that show where the line feeds go, and text on NETCONF username handling.

It also changes the terminology to "SSH client/server" and "NETCONF client/server" and folds in the verified errata for RFC 4742. IANA moved the TCP port 830 and the netconf subsystem name assignments, first made for RFC 4742, to refer to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the second edition. It swaps the shaky stop-sign trick for length counting and cleans up the wording.

left.title: Chunked framing
left.desc: Each chunk states its size. Used when both peers advertise :base:1.1.

right.title: End-of-message framing
right.desc: ]]>]]> after every message. Used when a peer supports only :base:1.0.
